text: The harbour town woke slowly that autumn. Fishing boats came in later than usual, their crews quiet after weeks of poor catches, and the market stalls along the quay opened one by one as the fog lifted. Marta, who had run the bakery on the corner for nearly thirty years, noticed the change before anyone else did: fewer people bought the second loaf, and the children who used to wait by the window for broken biscuits had started going straight to school. She did not complain about it. Instead she began baking smaller batches and giving the leftovers to the shelter on the hill, where the volunteers were grateful and the bread never went stale. By winter the town council had noticed too, and a short article in the local paper asked whether the old harbour could survive another bad season. Nobody had a clear answer, but the meetings in the church hall grew longer and louder, and for the first time in years people argued about the future instead of the past.
